blocks.x: One of the ironies of moviemaking is that a regular human life can seem too small to put onscreen. Living is the biggest thing any of us will ever do and yet it feels like a story about the ins and outs of everyday existence must be couched in some kind of premise or hook that can sell the story. To some degree, Rachel Morrison’s film Love Of Your Life has one. It’s a romance that explores what happens to fiercely independent nurse Maya (Margaret Qualley) after she meets-cute with adorably extroverted nerd Charlie (Gabriel Basso) when she’s 26 years old. Yet the heart of its story is anchored less in the rhythms of a romantic comedy or even a romantic drama than in the belief that the day-to-day realities of being a person are worthy of being immortalized.

With her gentle, small-scale sophomore feature, following the boxing drama The Fire Inside, Morrison is aiming for (if not quite hitting the highs of) the observational humanism that colors something like Celine Song’s Past Lives or Kelly Reichardt’s entire filmography. Several wrenching and dramatic things happen as Maya ages into her late 20s and early 30s, but Morrison presents them less as the beats of a classic melodrama and more as punctuation marks within a life that extends far beyond the logline you would use to sum it up. That makes Love Of Your Life hard to describe without spoiling it. It touches on topics ranging from marriage and family to grief and the impulse to escape reality. Yet the pleasure (and the tension) of watching it is the question of where Maya’s life will take her next—a path that’s predictable in its big beats but surprising in its small ones, anchored by Qualley’s luminously watchable screen presence.

The screenplay by Nyad writer Julia Cox is filled with well-observed grace notes, like Charlie’s complete non-jealousy around Maya’s best friendship with a guy she briefly dated in college (Patrick Schwarzenegger) or the way Maya mostly but perhaps not entirely connects with Charlie’s mom (a standout Catherine Keener) when he excitedly takes her home to meet his family. There’s an impromptu apartment celebration in the middle of a massive storm that feels like one of those perfect nights that could genuinely happen to a couple, not just something that could only take place in a movie. And the plot is rooted in a specific moment in time in a way that slowly but impactfully reveals itself.

Despite those highs, however, there are times the film pushes a touch too hard. The cast doesn’t always find a complete level of naturalism to their performances and the script occasionally falls back on overwritten exchanges and familiar platitudes, particularly in its second half, as Maya finds herself traveling the world and crossing paths with a handsome Londoner named Felix (Lanterns‘ Aaron Pierre). Still, the overall pacing is such that each time it feels like Love Of Your Life has settled into convention, it swerves in an unexpected direction. This isn’t a story with twists, exactly, but there are emotional shifts and reveals that arrive in ways that challenge our understanding of what the main characters have been running to and from.

In fact, Love Of Your Life both indulges and refutes the wave of Eat, Pray, Love-style travelogue romances that have been popping up everywhere. Working with DP Todd Banhazl, Morrison (herself an Oscar-nominated cinematographer) fills her screen with gorgeously dreamy montages of Portugal, London, Tokyo, and New Orleans. Yet Love Of Your Life doesn’t necessarily see the impulse to run away to find yourself as an inherently empowering one. Morrison is empathetic towards why her characters act the way they do, yet clear-eyed about the cost of their actions on the people around them. It all builds towards a climatic conversation that’s earnest without being overly sentimental.

Indeed, though romance drives the plot, Love Of Your Life is more of a character study of Maya than anything else. It’s her life that’s on display in all its moments, big and small, happy and sad. It’s a refreshingly grown-up perspective on a genre that has become increasingly overtaken by teen and young adult stories. The film’s title refers to the youthful optimism that you’ll one day find the person destined to be your great love. But, more importantly, it also refers to the idea that you need to learn to love your own life in both its tragedies and its ecstasies. After all, it’s the only one you’ve got.
Starring: Margaret Qualley, Gabriel Basso, Aaron Pierre, Patrick Schwarzenegger, Catherine Keener
